Cloud
KLOUD
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ānān and 'āb, and Greek nephelē, nephos)
From Old English clūd, which meant a mass of rock or a hill — the sense transferred to the piled mass of vapour by likeness of shape, so that the word for a crag became the word for a thunderhead. The Hebrew 'ānān is the covering cloud, and it is the word used of the pillar and of the glory; 'āb is the thick dark cloud of storm. Scripture's clouds are rarely weather and almost always presence.

Biblical Definition

In Scripture the cloud is chiefly the veil of the divine presence — the means by which a holy God comes near to a people who could not survive seeing Him plainly. The LORD went before Israel “in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way” (Exo 13:21), the same pillar that stood between the camp and the Egyptians, darkness to one and light to the other. When the tabernacle was finished the cloud covered the tent and the glory filled it, so that Moses was not able to enter; the cloud is thus both revelation and mercy, shewing that God is there and shielding the creature from what he cannot bear. The same cloud filled Solomon's temple, overshadowed the mount of transfiguration with the Father's voice out of it, and received the Lord out of the disciples' sight at the ascension (Act 1:9). And the promise of His return is in the same terms: this same Jesus shall so come in like manner, and every eye shall see him coming in the clouds of heaven. The cloud is also the emblem of the small beginning of great mercy — Elijah's servant saw only “a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand” (1Ki 18:44), and that hand-sized cloud broke a three-year drought. Hebrews turns the figure to the saints: we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1), a company so numerous that it is described as weather.

Webster 1828 Definition

The visible veil of the divine presence — the pillar that led Israel, the glory that filled tabernacle and temple, the overshadowing at the transfiguration, the chariot of the ascension and of the second coming — and the figure both of a small beginning of mercy and of the encompassing company of the saints.

CLOUD, n. 1. A collection of visible vapor, or watery particles, suspended in the atmosphere at some altitude.

2. In Scripture, the symbol and covering of the divine presence. The LORD went before them in a pillar of a cloud. Exodus 13. A cloud filled the house of the LORD. 1 Kings 8.

3. A great multitude; a collection so numerous as to resemble a cloud. So great a cloud of witnesses. Heb. 12.

4. That which obscures, darkens, or threatens; whence a cloud upon the countenance, and the day of clouds and thick darkness in the prophets. Joel 2.

5. To come in the clouds; the manner of our Lord's ascension and of his promised return. Behold, he cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him. Rev. 1.

Key Scripture

Exodus 13:21 — "And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:"

1 Kings 18:44 — "And it came to pass at the seventh time, that he said, Behold, there ariseth a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand. And he said, Go up, say unto Ahab, Prepare thy chariot, and get thee down, that the rain stop thee not."

Acts 1:9 — "And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight."

Hebrews 12:1 — "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,"

Modern Corruption

The cloud of glory is commonly reduced to a piece of ancient stage-scenery or a natural phenomenon dressed up by later writers, which empties the exodus, the temple, the transfiguration, and the ascension of the one thing they are all reporting.

expand to see more

The standard modern treatment explains the pillar of cloud as a volcanic plume, a caravan brazier, or a literary device added long after the events to lend authority to the sanctuary. Each of these begins from the assumption that God does not come near His people visibly, and then reconstructs the text to fit. Scripture presents the cloud as an event with witnesses, consequences, and a schedule — it moved and the camp moved, it settled and the camp stayed, it filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister. The narrative is not decorated with the cloud; the narrative depends on it. Once the cloud is explained away, the exodus becomes a migration, the tabernacle becomes architecture, and the ascension becomes a way of saying the disciples felt encouraged.

There is a second and gentler misuse inside the church: treating the cloud as a mood. Where the glory-cloud is invoked to describe an atmosphere in a meeting, or a sense of presence produced by music and expectation, the biblical thing is exchanged for a feeling that can be manufactured. The Scriptural cloud does not respond to technique; it comes and goes at God's appointment, it silences rather than excites, and it is consistently associated with the fear of the LORD. The Christian's access now is better than a cloud and not less — through the veil, that is to say, Christ's flesh — and the writer to the Hebrews sets the two side by side deliberately: not the mount that burned with fire and blackness and darkness and tempest, but mount Sion, and the city of the living God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ānān is the covering cloud of the pillar and the glory; 'āb is the thick storm cloud; 'arāphel is the thick darkness in which God is said to dwell. Greek nephelē is the single cloud, nephos the mass, used of the cloud of witnesses.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ānān (H6051) — cloud; the word of the pillar (Exo 13:21), of the cloud on the mercy seat (Lev 16:2), and of the glory filling the house.

Hebrew 'āb (H5645) — a thick dark cloud, the storm mass; the little cloud of 1Ki 18:44 and the clouds that are the dust of His feet (Nah 1:3).

Hebrew 'arāphel (H6205) — gross darkness, thick cloud; “the LORD said that he would dwell in the thick darkness” (1Ki 8:12).

Greek nephelē (G3507) — a cloud, a single defined cloud; the overshadowing cloud of the transfiguration and the cloud that received Him at the ascension.

Greek nephos (G3509) — a cloud mass; used once only, of the great cloud of witnesses in Heb 12:1, where the plural company is pictured as a single encompassing bank.

Usage

"Of the guiding and covering presence: the pillar of a cloud (Exo 13:21); the cloud covering the tent of the congregation (Exo 40:34); the cloud filling the house of the LORD (1Ki 8:10)."

"Of the coming and going of the Son: a bright cloud overshadowed them (Mat 17:5); a cloud received him out of their sight (Act 1:9); behold, he cometh with clouds (Rev 1:7)."

"Figuratively of multitude and of transience: so great a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1); your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away (Hos 6:4)."
